lessons.title: A countdown that knows when to stop
lessons.quiz: A loop starts with energy = 2, uses while energy >= 0, displays energy, then subtracts 1. What is displayed?
build_requirements: Read the requirement.
Make one change to the starter.
Run the checks.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.
lessons.semantic_reasoning: Condition is checked before each visit; >= includes boundary, and update moves toward termination. Fresh list, append-before-update, and return-after-loop prepare countdown.

source_evidence.text: A while loop repeats its body while a condition is true.
Python checks the condition before each repetition. If it is false at the beginning, the body runs zero times.

Here the number changes after each display.
```python
energy = 3
while energy > 0:
    print(energy)
    energy = energy - 1
```
The displayed values are 3, 2, and 1. After energy becomes 0, the condition 0 > 0 is false.
Indentation puts both instructions inside the repeated body. If the update were outside it, energy would stay 3 and this loop would not stop.
The condition decides whether a boundary is included. With energy >= 0, the same loop would also display 0 before stopping.

You can keep repeated results in a list instead of displaying them.
```python
steps = []
remaining = 2
while remaining > 0:
    steps.append(remaining)
    remaining = remaining - 1
print(steps)
```
This produces [2, 1]. append stores the current number before the update changes remaining.
In your function, create a fresh list for each call. Return it after the loop finishes, not during the first repetition.
Try a start of 0, then 1, then 4. These distinguish an empty loop, a single repetition, and several repetitions.

lessons.title: Number your research topics
lessons.quiz: You use enumerate(["Moon", "Sun"], start=5). Which number belongs to Sun?
build_requirements: Read the requirement.
Make one change to the starter.
Run the checks.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.
lessons.semantic_reasoning: enumerate supplies consecutive position/item pairs from the chosen start. Unpacking, f-string labels, append and empty input are visible.

source_evidence.text: enumerate lets a loop receive both a position number and an item.
Without a start argument, its counting begins at zero. Use start=1 when you want human-facing numbering.

Each repetition unpacks two values into the names before in.
```python
colors = ["Blue", "Gold"]
for number, color in enumerate(colors, start=1):
    print(number, color)
```
The displayed pairs are 1 Blue and 2 Gold. The original list still stores only the color strings.

An f-string can combine a number and a topic into one label.
```python
position = 3
name = "Clouds"
print(f"{position}. {name}")
```
This displays 3. Clouds. The dot and space are literal text inside the quotes.
Create a result list and append one formatted label per input item. Return the list after the loop.
An empty list gives enumerate no items to visit, so your result should stay empty. Do not add a placeholder topic.

lessons.title: Connect matching names and scores
lessons.quiz: When you loop over zip(["A", "B", "C"], [5, 7]), which pairs are visited?
build_requirements: Read the requirement.
Make one change to the starter.
Run the checks.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.
lessons.semantic_reasoning: zip pairs positions and stops at the shortest input; it does not fill or cross-product. Tuple construction and accumulation satisfy the equal-length Build contract.

source_evidence.text: zip pairs items from separate iterables by their position.

The first name pairs with the first score, then the second with the second.
```python
names = ["Mina", "Luis"]
points = [4, 9]
for name, point in zip(names, points):
    print(name, point)
```

A tuple can hold each pair as one result item. Parentheses and a comma form a two-item tuple.
```python
pair = ("Ari", 6)
print(pair)
```
Ordinary zip stops when the shortest input ends. It does not fill in missing scores.
This lesson’s function accepts equal-length lists, so no item should be dropped. A later validation step could reject mismatched lengths when input is not trusted.
Create a new result list. Append (name, score) for each pair, then return the result.
Two empty lists have no pairs and produce an empty result.

lessons.title: Give a function a useful default
lessons.quiz: repeat_label has times=2 as its default. What should repeat_label("Ready", times=0) return?
build_requirements: Read the requirement.
Make one change to the starter.
Run the checks.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.
lessons.semantic_reasoning: A supplied zero overrides a default; range(0) gives no repetitions. Keyword calls, fresh list, immutable default and loop accumulation support Build.

source_evidence.text: A default argument supplies a value when the caller leaves that argument out.

The default is written in the function definition.
```python
def add_bonus(score, bonus=3):
    return score + bonus
print(add_bonus(8))
print(add_bonus(8, 1))
```
The first call returns 11 because bonus is omitted. The second returns 9 because the explicit 1 replaces the default.

A keyword argument names the parameter it supplies.
```python
print(add_bonus(bonus=4, score=10))
```
Zero is a supplied value, not a missing argument. A caller can deliberately request no repetitions.
range(times) supplies the integers from zero up to, but not including, times. With range(3), a loop runs three times.
Build a fresh list inside the function. A default list would be shared across calls; this function needs only an immutable integer default.
Append text once per repetition and return the result. The input string is used as given, including an empty string.

lessons.title: Read a saved research note
lessons.quiz: The file contains "Moon\n". Why should read_note return the final line break too?
build_requirements: Read the requirement.
Make one change to the starter.
Run the checks.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.
lessons.semantic_reasoning: read returns file contents including line breaks; stripping would alter the requested data. open mode/encoding, with cleanup, paths and empty/missing difference are visible.

source_evidence.text: open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") opens a text file for reading. The encoding describes how stored bytes become characters.

A with block manages cleanup when its block finishes.
```python
with open("demo-note.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    text = handle.read()
print(text)
```
The name handle refers to the open file during the block. read() returns all remaining text, including line breaks.
This example needs a demo-note.txt file in the working directory. A relative path starts there; it is not automatically relative to whichever editor tab is open.
After the block, the file is closed even if reading raised an exception. The returned text remains usable because it is a separate string.
Reading mode does not erase the file. Writing mode "w" can replace existing contents, so do not use it for this reading task.
Return the text exactly: do not strip spaces or line breaks when the requirement is to preserve the note.

lessons.title: Change a local score without replacing another
lessons.quiz: level is 20 outside a function. The function receives level=3, reassigns its local level to 5, and returns 5. The caller ignores the return value. What is the outer level afterward?
build_requirements: Read the requirement.
Make one change to the starter.
Run the checks.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.
lessons.semantic_reasoning: Local assignment does not rebind an outer variable; ignoring a returned value leaves the outer binding unchanged. Function-local state and explicit caller assignment are taught.

source_evidence.text: A scope is the region where a name refers to a particular binding.
A function parameter creates a local name for that call. It can have the same spelling as a name outside the function without being the same binding.

This example uses the same spelling in two scopes.
```python
level = 20
def show_level(level):
    level = level + 2
    return level
print(show_level(3))
print(level)
```
The results are 5 and 20. The function changes its own local level binding, not the outer one.
Each call receives its own local parameter binding. Calling show_level(8) later returns 10 rather than continuing from the earlier local 5.
return sends a result to the caller. It does not automatically assign that result to a name outside the function.
If the caller wants to replace its stored value, it must assign the returned result itself.
In the practice, use the parameter score to calculate the result. Do not add global or depend on the unrelated outer value 100.

lessons.title: Collect readings until the stop signal
lessons.quiz: What changes if the zero branch uses continue instead of break for [3, 0, 8]?
build_requirements: Read the requirement.
Make one change to the starter.
Run the checks.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.
lessons.semantic_reasoning: continue skips one iteration; break ends the loop. Branch ordering, append placement and return-after-loop explain the changed zero behavior and Build.

source_evidence.text: continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration. The loop can still visit later items.
break exits the loop completely. Items after it are not visited by that loop.

This example skips a blank label but stops at a special word.
```python
labels = ["Moon", "", "Sun", "STOP", "Stars"]
kept = []
for label in labels:
    if label == "STOP":
        break
    if label == "":
        continue
    kept.append(label)

    def label(text):

    return label

```

    def add_two():

        return points
    return add_two
```

lessons.quiz: The original function returns input + 3. For input 4, why should the wrapper return 14 rather than 11?

Make one change to the starter.
Run the checks.
Explain why a changed input produces its result.

source_evidence.text: A decorator receives a function and returns the function that should be used in its place.
A wrapper can add behavior while calling the original function for its main work.

This example adds one to a result.
```python

    def wrapped(value):
        return function(value) + 1
    return wrapped

def square(value):
    return value * value

changed = plus_one(square)
print(changed(3))
```
The output is 10: square returns 9, then the wrapper adds one.
Writing @plus_one above a definition applies that decoration to the function name. It does not call the function with an input at definition time.
functools.wraps copies useful metadata from the original function to its wrapper, including the original name.
Use @wraps(function) above the nested wrapper. This helps inspection tools describe the wrapped operation accurately.
The practice contract is one positional input and a numeric result. A general-purpose wrapper would also need to forward other supported arguments.
Double the returned value, not the input. Those are different for functions that do more than multiply.

lessons.semantic_reasoning: finally runs when the with body exits normally or exceptionally without itself swallowing the error. contextmanager/yield protocol and one-yield contract prepare cleanup Build.

source_evidence.text: contextlib.contextmanager adapts a generator function into that protocol.
The generator runs to yield when the block begins. The yielded value becomes the value after as in the with statement.

Use try and finally so cleanup runs when control leaves the block.

def marked(log):

lessons.title: Choose an image for the available space

quiz.question: A source uses media="(min-width: 600px)". At exactly 600px, with a supported image format, is that condition satisfied?
choices: Yes, min-width includes the boundary
No, it starts at 601px
Only if img has the same filename
quiz.explanation: min-width includes the stated width. The source is eligible at 600px; its image still needs to load successfully.

lessons.rationale: Inclusive min-width selects at exact boundary; picture/source/img fallback and shared alt taught.

support_evidence.0: picture lets a browser choose an image source based on conditions while one img supplies the displayed image and alt text.
support_evidence.1: A source uses srcset for candidates. A media condition can select a different crop. ```html ```
support_evidence.2: The browser considers source elements in order and uses a suitable match. The img remains necessary as the fallback and the image element itself.
support_evidence.3: min-width includes its boundary. This example selects its wide candidate at 800px as well as wider viewports.
support_evidence.4: Changing the crop to suit the composition is called art direction. It differs from offering several resolutions of the same image.
support_evidence.5: Place alt on img, not source. The description should remain appropriate for every crop.
support_evidence.6: The exercise filenames are placeholders. Markup checks cannot prove that the files exist, that the crop is useful, or which resource a real browser downloads.

lessons.title: Open and close a named dialog

quiz.question: You add open to dialog but never call showModal(). Does that alone make the background inert?
choices: Yes, every visible dialog is modal
No, open alone displays a nonmodal dialog
Only when the heading is h2
quiz.explanation: The modal behavior comes from showModal(), not merely the presence of open.

lessons.rationale: Modal vs nonmodal and opener/close syntax are shown, but quiz-critical inert is not defined in plain words.

support_evidence.0: dialog represents a dialog box. Merely adding open shows it nonmodally; showModal() opens it modally in the browser’s top layer.
support_evidence.1: A modal dialog makes the background inert while it is open. A details disclosure does not do that.
support_evidence.2: Name the dialog with aria-labelledby pointing to its visible heading. Do not put tabindex on the dialog itself.
support_evidence.3:
A button can request opening through a small event handler. ```html

Packing tip

 ``` This demonstration uses a local inline handler; larger apps can attach a listener from their script.
support_evidence.4:
A form with method="dialog" closes its containing dialog rather than submitting a network request.
```html
<form method="dialog"><button>Close tip</button></form>
```

support_evidence.6: After closing, verify focus returns to the opener. Check opening, keyboard movement, Escape and the visible close control in a real browser; attributes alone do not prove that experience.

lessons.title: A restricted embedded document

quiz.question: An iframe has sandbox="". You remove the entire attribute. Is the result still equally restricted?
choices: Yes, both contain no permission words
No, removing sandbox removes those sandbox restrictions
Yes, srcdoc always implies a full sandbox
quiz.explanation: The presence of sandbox enables its restrictions. An empty value grants no optional permissions; absence does not enable sandboxing.

lessons.rationale: Empty sandbox enables restrictions while omission does not; srcdoc escaping and title shown without permission grants.

support_evidence.0: iframe embeds a separate document. Its title helps identify the frame to assistive technology.
support_evidence.1:
srcdoc supplies inline HTML instead of fetching an external page.
```html
<iframe title="Example note" sandbox srcdoc="<p>A quiet note.</p>"></iframe>
```
support_evidence.2: An empty sandbox attribute enables restrictions without granting optional permissions. Omitting sandbox is not the same as writing it empty.
support_evidence.3: Permission tokens can relax specific restrictions. This exercise needs no scripts, forms, popups or same-origin access, so it grants none.
support_evidence.4: Do not combine allow-scripts and allow-same-origin casually for same-origin untrusted content; that can undermine the intended restriction.
support_evidence.5: Sandboxing is not sanitization or a blanket network firewall. Treat HTML input deliberately, use a suitable content policy, and grant only the abilities actually needed.
support_evidence.6: The practice uses only fixed, harmless text. Its checks inspect the embedding contract, not every browser security boundary or arbitrary hostile document.

build_task: Embed the harmless note using srcdoc, give the frame a title, and keep an empty sandbox attribute with no permission tokens.

lessons.title: When two rules disagree

quiz.question: A paragraph has class="tip". The stylesheet first says .tip { color: blue; } and later p { color: red; }. What happens if you move the p rule above the .tip rule?
choices: The paragraph changes from red to blue
The paragraph stays blue
The paragraph inherits its parent’s color
quiz.explanation: The class selector wins over the element selector in either order here. Source order breaks a tie; these selectors do not have equal specificity.

lessons.rationale: Same-layer class specificity outranks element despite source order; inherited body color applies where unoverridden.

support_evidence.0: A CSS rule affects only elements its selector matches.
support_evidence.1: When matching rules set the same property, the cascade chooses a winner. Here we compare ordinary stylesheet rules in the same layer, without inline styles or !important.
support_evidence.5: In the practice, the footer has no color rule of its own, so it can inherit the body color. Give notice paragraphs their own class rule instead of changing every paragraph.

lessons.title: Styles that follow interaction

quiz.question: A form shows a helpful border only on input:hover. A person uses Tab to reach the field without moving a mouse. What is missing?
choices: A focus indicator for keyboard interaction
A second hover rule with a darker color
A disabled attribute on the input
quiz.explanation: Hover depends on pointing interaction. Keyboard focus is a different state, so a visible focus style is needed without disabling the field.

lessons.rationale: Pointing hover differs from focus; visible outline and disabled-state opacity/availability distinction taught.

support_evidence.0: A pseudo-class selects an element in a particular state. It begins with a colon.
support_evidence.1:
:hover matches when a pointing device is over an element. A keyboard user may never hover over it.
```css
a:hover { text-decoration: underline; }
```
support_evidence.2: :focus matches the element receiving keyboard input. :focus-visible matches when the browser decides a visible focus indicator is needed.
support_evidence.4: Do not remove the browser’s focus indicator unless you provide another visible one. A hover style alone is not a keyboard focus indicator.
support_evidence.5:
:disabled matches a disabled control.
```css
button:disabled { opacity: 0.6; }
```
The HTML disabled attribute controls availability; dimming alone does not disable a button.
support_evidence.6: For the practice, keyboard-tab to the input and look for the outline. Inspect the disabled button separately. Automated focus checks do not prove every keyboard interaction works.

lessons.title: Normal flow and overflowing content

quiz.question: A 200px box contains a 400px line. You replace overflow: auto with overflow: hidden. What changes for the reader?
choices: The box automatically widens to 400px
Overflowing content is clipped without a user scrollbar
The text is deleted from the document
quiz.explanation: Hidden clips what lies outside the box without offering normal user scrolling. The underlying content still exists, and the fixed box width does not automatically change.

lessons.rationale: Hidden clips without user scrolling while auto allows it; display block and width constraint support task.

support_evidence.0: Normal flow is the ordinary arrangement of boxes before special positioning or layout systems change it.
support_evidence.1: A block box normally starts on a new line. Inline content can share a line with surrounding text.
support_evidence.2:
display changes the box behavior without changing the HTML meaning.
```css
.tag { display: block; }
```
Two spans with class="tag" now start on separate lines.
support_evidence.3: Content can be wider than its container. That is overflow, not a request to make the container wider.
support_evidence.5: overflow: hidden clips content without showing scrollbars for the user. For a reading window, that can hide information the reader needs.
support_evidence.6: The practice provides one long line. Keep its width and text, constrain the outer window, and allow the reader to reach the end by scrolling.

lessons.title: How flex items share space

quiz.question: Two items have equal bases but flex-grow: 0. The row has spare space. What happens?
choices: The items automatically split all spare space
They do not grow to consume that space
They disappear from the row
quiz.explanation: A zero grow factor declines positive free space. Container alignment may position the remaining space, but it does not make these items grow.

lessons.rationale: Grow factor controls free space but zero-factor behavior tested by quiz is implicit rather than explained.

support_evidence.0: Flex container rules arrange a row; flex item rules decide how each child uses its share of space.
support_evidence.1: flex-basis gives an item’s starting size along the main axis before free space is distributed.
support_evidence.2: flex-grow controls how positive free space is shared. Equal grow factors share that free space equally; they do not always imply equal final widths when starting sizes differ.
support_evidence.3: flex-shrink controls shrinking when space is short. Shrink distribution also depends on the starting basis size.
support_evidence.4:
With equal starting bases and equal factors, these simple items stay equal.
```css
.item { flex: 1 1 80px; min-width: 0; }
```
The shorthand order is grow, shrink, basis.
support_evidence.5: min-width: 0 allows the items to shrink below their usual minimum-content width. In real layouts, still protect readable content from clipping.
support_evidence.6: The practice has no gaps, padding or borders, so its equal widths isolate item sizing rather than extra box space.

build_task: Let two items start from a 120px basis, grow equally into spare space, and shrink equally when the row is narrower.
Run the checks.

lessons.title: Stacking contexts keep layers together

quiz.question: A badge has z-index: 500 inside a parent at0. An overlapping sibling context is at1. What is the right first investigation?
choices: Increase the badge to5000 without inspecting parents
Inspect the parent stacking contexts
Remove the badge text
quiz.explanation: The badge’s local number cannot outrank its parent’s sibling context. The relevant ordering is between the parent groups.

lessons.rationale: Child z-index cannot escape parent context; positioned fixture and parent-level correction explained.

support_evidence.0: z-index orders elements within a stacking context; it is not one global ranking for the entire page.
support_evidence.1: A positioned element with a non-auto z-index creates a stacking context. Its descendants are ordered inside that group.
support_evidence.2: A child with z-index: 999 cannot escape a parent context below a sibling context. Raise the appropriate parent when the whole group should be above.
support_evidence.3: Other properties, including transforms and opacity below one, can also create stacking contexts. Inspect ancestors before repeatedly increasing a child’s z-index.
support_evidence.4: The practice already positions two overlapping groups. Change the first group’s stacking level, not just the badge’s large number.

lessons.title: Spacing that follows reading direction

quiz.question: A horizontal note changes from dir=ltr to dir=rtl. What happens to padding-inline-start?
choices: It stays on the physical left
It maps to the right
It becomes a margin
quiz.explanation: Inline-start follows the beginning of the inline writing direction. In horizontal RTL text that side is the right.

lessons.rationale: Logical inline start follows horizontal writing direction; logical padding example teaches both sides.

support_evidence.0: Physical left and right stay on those sides. Logical inline-start and inline-end follow the text’s writing direction.
support_evidence.1: For horizontal left-to-right text, inline-start is left. For horizontal right-to-left text, inline-start is right.
support_evidence.2:
Logical spacing can adapt without separate left and right rules.
```css
.note { padding-inline-start: 16px; padding-inline-end: 4px; }
```
support_evidence.3: The HTML dir attribute expresses text direction. CSS logical properties respond to that direction; they do not translate the content.
support_evidence.4: Block-start and block-end follow the other layout axis. Vertical writing modes change the mapping, so do not define logical properties as permanent synonyms for top or left.
support_evidence.5: The practice uses horizontal writing only. Check both directions instead of looking at one note and assuming the other adapts.

lessons.title: Organize normal rules into layers

quiz.question: For normal author rules, an early layer has an ID selector and a later layer has a matching element selector. Which comparison comes first?
choices: Layer precedence, so the later layer wins
Specificity, so the ID always wins across layers
Alphabetical order of selector names
quiz.explanation: Normal layer precedence is considered before selector specificity. Specificity does not allow an earlier layer to jump above a later layer.

lessons.rationale: Normal layer precedence is resolved before specificity; layer order and exception boundaries explicit.

support_evidence.0: Cascade layers give groups of styles an explicit precedence before specificity is compared within a group.
support_evidence.2: The order statement establishes the order of named layers. Reopening a layer adds rules to that layer rather than moving it later.
support_evidence.3: Normal unlayered author rules outrank normal layered author rules. Keep that distinction in mind when introducing layers into an existing stylesheet.
support_evidence.4: Important declarations reverse layer priority. This practice deliberately uses no !important, inline styles or animations, so it isolates normal stylesheet rules.
support_evidence.5: The practice’s selectors already match the same paragraph. Change the declared layer order rather than increasing selector specificity.
